intro.html: Learning comes with its own cast of characters: the beginner, the dabbler, the young wonder, the expert with fine taste, the master performer and the person who seems to know a little about everything. Two more words describe learning worn too heavily, and one describes teaching itself.

Beginners and dabblers: novice, dilettante. Young talent: prodigy, precocious. Experts: connoisseur (fine taste), virtuoso (performance), polymath (many subjects), erudite (deep reading). Learning overdone: pedantic (fussing over small rules) and didactic (teaching, often preachy).

words.def: having or showing great knowledge from reading and study
words.ex: The {erudite} librarian could answer questions about almost any book on the shelves.
words.ctx: Though he never went to college, Grandpa Gus was {erudite}; he had read every history book in the town library and could talk about ancient Rome for hours.
words.etym: From Latin eruditus, “instructed,” from erudire, “to polish, to teach”: e (out) + rudis (rough, untaught). Study takes the roughness out.

mn.cue: “READ IT!”: he has read them all
mn.text: Ask Professor Edwin about any book in the library and he smiles: “Read it!” He has read them all; he is {erudite}.

scene.alt: An old professor beside a tall stack of books tells a surprised teen that he has read the book she is holding.

words.def: too concerned with small details and rules, often to show off learning
words.ex: My {pedantic} cousin corrected my grammar in the middle of my birthday toast.
words.ctx: The tour guide knew a great deal, but she was so {pedantic} that she spent ten minutes on the difference between two kinds of nails while the visitors fidgeted.
words.etym: From pedant, from Italian pedante, “a schoolteacher.”

mn.text: Dan stops the soccer game to read out the rule about exactly how round the ball must be. Dan is {pedantic}.

scene.alt: A boy named Dan reads a rule book aloud in the middle of a soccer game while his bored friends wait.

words.def: meant to teach a lesson, often in a preachy way
words.ex: The picture book was so {didactic} that every page ended with a lesson about brushing your teeth.
words.ctx: The film had fine actors, but it felt {didactic} rather than entertaining; every scene paused so that someone could deliver a little lecture on saving water.
words.etym: From Greek didaktikos, “good at teaching,” from didaskein, “to teach.”

mn.cue: DID-ACT-ic: every ACT stops for a LESSON
mn.text: The class play did act out a story, but every scene stopped for a lecture: “And the lesson is…” The play is {didactic}.

scene.alt: A teen in a costume crown stops the class play to deliver a lesson while her classmates yawn.

words.def: an expert judge of things that need fine taste, such as food, art or music
words.ex: A cheese {connoisseur} can tell where a cheese was made from a single bite.
words.ctx: Most visitors glanced at the paintings and moved on, but Felix was a {connoisseur}: he could name the painter, the year and even the kind of brush used.
words.etym: From old French connoisseur, “one who knows,” from Latin cognoscere, “to come to know.”

mn.text: Victor takes one lick of each ice cream cone and names the flavor and the farm it came from. He is a {connoisseur}.

scene.alt: A man with a monocle tastes an ice cream cone and names its flavor while the shopkeeper claps.

words.def: a person who dabbles in a subject or an art without serious study
words.ex: He calls himself a painter, but he is a {dilettante} who finishes about one picture a year.
words.ctx: Real gardeners spend years learning their soil, but Marcus was only a {dilettante}: he planted whatever looked pretty at the store and lost interest by July.
words.etym: From Italian dilettante, “a lover of the arts,” from dilettare, “to delight.”

mn.text: Pip dillydallies: guitar on Monday, painting on Tuesday, chess on Wednesday. He dabbles in each and masters none: he is a {dilettante}.

scene.alt: A boy shrugs among a half-tried guitar, a painting, a chess piece and a tennis racket.

words.def: a beginner; someone new to a skill or activity
words.ex: As a {novice} skater, Lin spent more time on the ice than on her feet.
words.ctx: The chess club welcomed everyone, from {novices} still learning how the knight moves to old masters who had played for fifty years.
words.etym: From Latin novicius, “new,” from novus (new), the root of novel and renovate.

mn.text: Jamal is new on the ice: wobbly knees, waving arms, one big bump. He is a {novice} skater.

scene.alt: A man wobbles and falls on the ice for the first time while a teen skates easily nearby.

words.def: a young person with an amazing talent
words.ex: At six, the piano {prodigy} played a concert in a packed hall.
words.ctx: Most children her age were learning to add, but Ivy was a math {prodigy}: at eight, she was solving puzzles that stumped her brother’s high school teacher.
words.etym: From Latin prodigium, “a wonder, a sign of things to come.”

mn.cue: PRO-digy: a PRO, and only three
mn.text: Little Theo is only three, yet he plays the violin like a pro. The crowd can’t believe it: he is a {prodigy}!

scene.alt: A tiny boy holds up his violin on stage while a man in the audience claps in amazement.

words.def: showing skills or behavior unusually early for one’s age
words.ex: The {precocious} toddler could read the cereal box before she turned three.
words.ctx: Most kindergartners just ask for juice, but {precocious} little Theo asked the waiter whether the orange juice was freshly squeezed.
words.etym: From Latin praecox, “ripening early”: prae (before) + coquere (to cook, to ripen).
words.note: Precocious can praise a child’s early skill, or tease a child for acting older than his years.

mn.text: Ivy is only four, yet she cooks a whole breakfast: pancakes, eggs and toast. She is {precocious}: ripe early.

scene.alt: A little girl in a chef's hat proudly serves breakfast in a pan while her astonished mother looks on.

words.def: a person who knows a great deal about many different subjects
words.ex: A true {polymath}, Professor Edwin has written books on birds, bridges and old poems.
words.ctx: Ada was a {polymath}: she designed bridges by day, played the cello in the city orchestra by night and still found time to write a history of maps.
words.etym: From Greek polymathes, “having learned much”: poly (much, many) + manthanein (to learn), the same root as mathematics.

mn.text: Ada knows math, music, maps, stars and many more subjects besides: she is a {polymath}.

scene.alt: A cheerful woman stands among a globe, a telescope, a violin, books and a blackboard of math.

words.def: a person with outstanding skill, especially in playing music
words.ex: The violin {virtuoso} played so fast that her bow seemed to blur.
words.ctx: Many players can stumble through that hard passage, but only a {virtuoso} like Lin makes it sound easy, as if her fingers were simply dancing on the keys.
words.etym: From Italian virtuoso, “skilled, excellent,” from Latin virtus, “excellence, worth.”

mn.text: Lin’s fingers race over the piano keys like a speeding train: choo-choo, oh so fast! She is a {virtuoso}.

scene.alt: A woman plays the piano at dazzling speed while a grandmother claps.

after.cap: Six kinds of learners, from first try to mastery.

after.html: Watch the tone. Erudite praises deep learning, but pedantic criticizes someone who fusses over small points to show off. Didactic simply means meant to teach, though it often hints at preachiness. And precocious cuts both ways: it can praise a child’s early talent or tease a child for acting like a little grown-up.

opts.s: Dev had played the tuba for only a week, and like most {novices}, he squeaked more than he played.
opts.why: Someone a week into learning is a beginner: a novice.

items.q: Which word is always a compliment?
items.why: Erudite praises deep learning. Pedantic criticizes fussing over small points, a dilettante only dabbles, and didactic often hints at preachiness.

items.q: True or false: precocious can describe a child who acts older than her age.
items.why: True. Precocious means developed unusually early, in skills or in behavior: ripe before her time.

items.q: A coffee ______ can taste the difference between beans grown on two sides of the same mountain. Which word fits?
items.why: An expert judge of taste is a connoisseur. A dilettante only dabbles, and a novice is just starting out.
Poly- means many, as in polygon (many angles). A polymath has learned many subjects.

items.q: Type the word for a beginner, which comes from Latin novus (new).
items.why: A novice is someone new to a skill: a beginner.
